slide.title: Can They Hear You?
slide.body: Three stacked waveforms: voice (large, teal), music (small, grey), sound effects (small, light blue). Small tag: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 12.

scenes.voiceover: Viewers often forgive a small visual problem. They rarely forgive a voice they cannot hear. Sound is half of your video, and the export is the version people actually watch. This is capstone step two.

slide.title: Sound, Music and Export Settings
slide.body: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 12 of 14

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, you built your rough cut. Now you make it sound right, and export it for the places people will watch it.

slide.title: Three layers of sound
slide.body: Three stacked tracks: Voice (most important, largest) · Music (mood and pace) · Sound effects (door, waves, coffee pour).

scenes.voiceover: Most short videos have three layers of sound. The voice, from your narration or avatar, is the most important. Music sets the mood and the pace. And sound effects, like a door, waves or a coffee pour, make generated clips feel real.

slide.title: Balancing levels
slide.body: 1. Voice first: loud, clear, no distortion · 2. Music well below the voice, adjust by ear · 3. Automatic lowering under speech, if your editor has it

scenes.voiceover: The voice must always be clear. So set the voice first, loud and clear without distortion. Then bring the music in well below it, and adjust by ear. If your editor can lower music automatically under speech, use it.

scenes.stock_query: person listening to phone speaker closely
scenes.voiceover: Then listen twice, on phone speakers and on headphones. A mix that sounds good on headphones can sound unclear on a phone.

slide.title: Check the music licence
slide.body: Commercial use allowed? · Which platforms? · Credit required? Note: royalty-free does not always mean free for any use.

scenes.voiceover: Now music. Only use music whose licence allows your use. Royalty-free does not always mean free for any use. Ask three questions. Can you use it commercially? On which platforms? Do you need to credit the creator?

scenes.on_screen_text: Save the licence with your project
scenes.voiceover: Editors, stock libraries and AI music tools each have their own terms, and they change. Save a copy of the licence with your project. And never use a popular song just because you own a copy of it.

slide.title: Two versions
slide.body: Left: 16:9 horizontal frame, websites and presentations. Right: 9:16 vertical frame, short-form social apps. Note: check each platform's current guidance.

scenes.voiceover: Next, export. Plan two versions. A horizontal version, sixteen by nine, for websites and presentations. And a vertical version, nine by sixteen, for short-form social apps. Platform requirements change, so check each platform's current guidance.

slide.title: The safe area
slide.body: Vertical phone frame with grey blocks at the bottom and right edge for app buttons. A dashed teal box in the centre labelled safe area, with captions inside it.

scenes.voiceover: On vertical apps, buttons and text cover parts of the screen, especially the bottom and the right side. So keep captions and important details inside the central safe area.

scenes.on_screen_text: Music is the room, not the speaker
scenes.voiceover: Mixing sound is like a dinner conversation in a restaurant. The music is the background noise of the room. If it becomes too loud, nobody at the table can hear the person speaking, however interesting they are.

scenes.stock_query: surf lesson for beginners on sunny beach
scenes.voiceover: Let's see an example. Lucas runs a surf school in Florianópolis, Brazil. The school is made up for this lesson. His eighty-second video is edited. Now he works on sound and export.

slide.title: Voice and music
slide.body: 1. Voice clear and steady; hum removed · 2. Calm acoustic track · 3. Licence read: commercial use allowed, credit optional · 4. Copy saved in the project folder

scenes.voiceover: First, he makes the voice clear and steady, and removes a short hum with noise reduction. Then he chooses a calm acoustic track. He reads the licence. For his track, commercial use is allowed and credit is optional. He saves a copy in his project folder.

slide.title: Lucas's mix
slide.body: Timeline: voice track across the video; music track low throughout, slightly higher in the first 4 seconds; two small sound-effect blocks labelled waves and board on water.

scenes.voiceover: He places the music under the whole video, well below the voice. He raises it slightly only in the four-second opening, where there is no narration. He adds two sound effects. Waves on the beach shot, and a board hitting the water.

scenes.stock_query: man listening to video on smartphone at beach
scenes.voiceover: Then he listens on his phone. The music hides the word beginners. So he lowers the music further, until every word is clear.

slide.title: Horizontal, then vertical
slide.body: Left: 16:9 frame of a surfer, 1080p, exported. Right: 9:16 frame, reframed so the surfer is centred, captions moved up into the safe area.

scenes.voiceover: He exports a sixteen by nine version at ten eighty p. Then he duplicates the project, changes it to nine by sixteen, and reframes each clip, so the surfer stays in the centre. He moves the captions up into the safe area, and exports the vertical version.

A common mistake is loud music that sounds exciting on headphones, but hides the voice on a phone. Another is changing the aspect ratio without reframing, so subjects are cut off and captions sit under app buttons.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Voice first; test on a phone. 2. Check and save the music licence. 3. 16:9 and 9:16, reframed, captions in the safe area.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the voice comes first. Music and sound effects sit clearly below it, and you test the mix on phone speakers. Second, use only music whose licence allows your use, and save a copy of the licence. Third, export a horizontal and a vertical version, reframe each shot, and keep captions inside the safe area.

Now it is your turn, with capstone step two. Add music and one to three sound effects, balance the levels on a phone and on headphones, and save the music licence. Then export one horizontal and one vertical version. It takes about thirty-five minutes. Next lesson: Publishing Responsibly, Disclosure, Consent and Rights.
